slides.storyContext: The negatively charged comb induces a positive charge on the paper (polarization). Opposite charges attract. Paper bits are pulled toward the comb—and may stick if the attractive force is strong enough.

slides.title: Force on Paper Scrap
slides.storyContext: A small paper scrap gains a net charge of 0.1 nC when near the comb. The comb's charge is 1.6 nC, distance 1 cm.

example.problem: Calculate the attractive force.

slides.inSimpleWords: Even tiny charges separated by small distances can create meaningful forces.

slides.title: Electric Field

points.label: Definition
points.text: Electric field E at a point is the force per unit positive test charge: E = F / q_test, with units N/C or V/m.

points.label: Field from a point charge
points.text: For a point charge Q at distance r: E = k Q / r^2, directed radially outward if Q > 0, inward if Q < 0.

points.label: Superposition
points.text: Net field from multiple charges is the vector sum of individual fields. Fields add like vectors.

image.alt: Electric Field — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.inSimpleWords: The electric field is the influence a charge spreads around itself. It tells you what force a test charge would feel at any point.

slides.title: Field from Anjali's Comb
slides.storyContext: Calculate the electric field at distance 2 cm from Anjali's charged comb.
slides.inSimpleWords: The electric field strength drops quickly with distance (inverse square law).

slides.title: Field Lines and Gauss's Law

points.label: Field lines
points.text: Imaginary lines showing the direction of E. They start on positive charges and end on negative charges. Density of lines ∝ field strength.

points.label: Gauss's Law
points.text: Total electric flux through a closed surface = Q_enclosed / ε₀, where ε₀ = 8.85 × 10^-12 C^2/(N·m^2). Mathematically: ∮ E·dA = Q_enclosed / ε₀.

points.label: Significance
points.text: Gauss's law is a powerful tool for finding E when charge distribution is symmetric (sphere, cylinder, plate).

slides.inSimpleWords: Field lines are invisible paths showing the direction of the field. Gauss's law lets you count the total field passing through a surface.

image.alt: Field Lines and Gauss's Law — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: Visualizing Field Lines
slides.storyContext: Ravi helps Anjali visualize the electric field around the comb. 'Imagine invisible arrows radiating outward from the negatively charged comb, pointing inward (toward the negative charge). Paper bits align with these invisible lines, getting attracted inward.'

slides.title: The Lightning Connection
slides.storyContext: Ravi tells Anjali about lightning: huge charges (millions of coulombs) build up in clouds. When the potential difference reaches millions of volts, a conducting path (lightning) forms and discharge happens explosively.

slides.title: Multiple Charges and Superposition

points.label: Superposition principle
points.text: Net force on a charge is vector sum of forces from all other charges.

points.label: Vector addition
points.text: Forces must be added as vectors (magnitude and direction), not scalars.

example.problem: Two charges q1 = +2 μC and q2 = +2 μC are 0.1 m apart. A test charge q_t = +1 μC is placed at the midpoint. Find net force.
example.solution: Each charge exerts F = (9×10^9 × 2×10^-6 × 1×10^-6) / (0.05)^2 = 7.2 N repulsive, pointing away. Net F = 7.2 - 7.2 = 0 (symmetric cancellation).

slides.inSimpleWords: When multiple charges push on one charge, add all forces as vectors.

slides.title: Conductors vs Insulators

points.label: Conductors
points.text: Metals (copper, aluminum) have free electrons. In electrostatic equilibrium, E = 0 inside, all charge sits on the surface. E is perpendicular to surface.

points.label: Insulators
points.text: Non-metals (rubber, glass) have electrons bound to atoms. E penetrates; charges remain wherever placed.

points.label: Charging by induction
points.text: Bringing a charged object near an uncharged conductor causes charges to separate, creating an induced charge. No actual charge transfer.

slides.inSimpleWords: In metals, charges are free to move and rush to the surface. In rubber or glass, charges stay put.

image.alt: Conductors vs Insulators — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: The Charged Plastic Comb: Conductor or Insulator?
slides.storyContext: Anjali's plastic comb is an insulator. The negative charge stays where friction created it—on the surface. If the comb were metal, charge would redistribute instantly to the outer surface.

slides.title: Solved Problem: Three Charges in a Row

example.problem: Three point charges: q1 = +1 μC at x = 0, q2 = −2 μC at x = 0.1 m, q3 = +1 μC at x = 0.2 m. Find the net force on q2.
example.solution: Force on q2 from q1: F₁ = k (1 × 10^-6) (2 × 10^-6) / (0.1)^2 = 1.8 N, pointing right (attractive). Force on q2 from q3: F₃ = k (1 × 10^-6) (2 × 10^-6) / (0.1)^2 = 1.8 N, pointing left (attractive). Net force on q2 = 1.8 − 1.8 = 0 N (the two forces cancel).

slides.inSimpleWords: When a charge sits between two others of opposite sign, the forces can balance completely.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Three Charges in a Row — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: Challenge: Distance and Force
slides.storyContext: If Anjali moves the paper scrap 2 cm away from her comb (instead of 1 cm), how does the force change?

points.text: Use Coulomb's law inverse-square relationship: F ∝ 1/r².

example.problem: If r doubles, how does F change?
example.solution: F_new = k q1 q2 / (2r)^2 = k q1 q2 / (4r^2) = F_old / 4. Force drops to 1/4 of original!

slides.inSimpleWords: Doubling the distance reduces force to 1/4. This inverse-square law is fundamental to gravity and electricity.

points.text: Anjali rubs a balloon on her dry hair and it sticks to the ceiling. The balloon acquires a negative charge of 5 μC. Assume the ceiling has an induced positive charge of 5 μC over an area of 0.01 m^2. Estimate the average electric field between the balloon and ceiling, assuming they are 0.05 m apart. (Hint: E ≈ σ / ε₀, where σ is surface charge density.)

example.problem: What is the electric field and attractive force?
example.solution: Charge density σ = 5 × 10^-6 / 0.01 = 5 × 10^-4 C/m^2. Electric field E = σ / ε₀ ≈ (5 × 10^-4) / (8.85 × 10^-12) ≈ 5.65 × 10^7 N/C. Force F = qE = (5 × 10^-6) × (5.65 × 10^7) ≈ 0.28 N ≈ 28 grams-force, enough to hold the balloon.

image.alt: Challenge: The Balloon Trick — Electric Charges and Fields

slides.title: Static Electricity Dangers
slides.storyContext: Ravi tells Anjali about ESD (electrostatic discharge). When you walk on a carpet and touch metal, sparks fly. For electronics, these sparks can destroy circuits. That's why technicians wear wrist straps.

slides.title: ESD Risk Assessment
slides.storyContext: A technician touches a microchip with 10,000 V static charge. The chip's breakdown voltage is 5,000 V.

example.problem: Is the chip safe?
example.solution: No. The ESD voltage (10 kV) exceeds the breakdown voltage (5 kV), so the chip will be damaged or destroyed. Modern chips are vulnerable to ESD damage even at voltages humans cannot feel.

slides.inSimpleWords: Static electricity, though invisible, has real destructive power.

slides.title: Electroscope Experiment
slides.storyContext: An electroscope detects charge by observing if two thin metal leaves repel each other.

example.problem: If leaves repel, what can you conclude?
example.solution: Both leaves must have the same type of charge (both positive or both negative). Mutual repulsion is proof of like charges.

slides.inSimpleWords: Simple experiments reveal charge without complex math.

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Electric charge exists in two types—positive and negative—and is conserved.
Coulomb's law: F = k q₁ q₂ / r², the inverse-square law for electrostatic force.
Electric field E = F / q_test measures the field strength; field lines show its direction.
Gauss's law: ∮ E·dA = Q_enclosed / ε₀, a powerful symmetry tool.
In conductors, charges rearrange to make E = 0 inside; in insulators, E penetrates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Charges push and pull via electric fields. The closer or stronger, the bigger the force. Metals hide the field inside; insulators let it through.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Electric Charges and Fields

subject: Physics
title: The Bottled Lightning: Capacitors
hook: Ravi shows Anjali how a capacitor stores electric energy—and why camera flashes need them to survive.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student exploring energy storage in electrical circuits

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor demonstrating capacitor function with a real camera flash

slides.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
slides.storyContext: When Ravi's camera flash fails, Anjali asks why. 'The capacitor is discharged,' he says. 'A capacitor is like a battery that can store and release electrical energy almost instantly.'

image.alt: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: The Camera Flash
slides.storyContext: Anjali is at a wedding in Mumbai. The photographer's flash quits mid-ceremony. Ravi explains: 'The capacitor inside the flash stores electrical energy when the camera is idle. When you press the shutter, the capacitor releases all that energy at once, creating a bright pulse of light. Without capacitors, we couldn't have instant, bright flashes.'

image.alt: The Camera Flash — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Electric Potential

points.label: Definition
points.text: Electric potential V at a point is the work per unit positive charge to bring a test charge from infinity to that point: V = W / q, with units volts (V) = J/C.

points.label: Potential from a point charge
points.text: For a point charge Q: V = k Q / r. The potential is a scalar (not a vector). Reference point is at infinity (V = 0).

points.label: Potential difference
points.text: Voltage U_AB = V_A − V_B. This is the work per unit charge to move a charge from B to A.

image.alt: Electric Potential — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.inSimpleWords: Potential is the 'height' of the electric field. Higher potential means more energy per charge. Moving against the field (uphill) costs work; moving downhill releases energy.

slides.title: Potential as Energy Currency
slides.storyContext: Ravi tells Anjali to think of potential like altitude. A charge at high potential (mountain top) has more potential energy than one at low potential (valley). Moving downhill releases energy.

slides.title: Potential Near a Charge
slides.storyContext: A positive charge of 1 μC sits at a point. What is the potential at distance 10 cm?
slides.inSimpleWords: Potential near a charge can be quite large. Moving a test charge from here to infinity would release energy.

slides.title: Equipotentials and Relationship to E

points.label: Equipotential surfaces
points.text: Surfaces where V is constant. No work is needed to move a charge along an equipotential. E is always perpendicular to equipotential surfaces.

points.label: E and V relationship
points.text: Electric field is the negative gradient of potential: E = −dV/dr (in 1D). In other words, E points in the direction of steepest V decrease.

points.label: Uniform field
points.text: Between two parallel plates separated by distance d at potentials V_A and V_B: E = |V_A − V_B| / d.

slides.inSimpleWords: Field lines are perpendicular to equipotentials. The field points downhill (from high to low potential).

image.alt: Equipotentials and Relationship to E — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Two Charged Plates: Inside a Capacitor
slides.storyContext: Ravi shows Anjali the inside of a broken capacitor: two metal plates separated by thin insulation. One plate is positive (high potential), one is negative (low potential). The uniform field between them is what stores energy.

slides.title: Field Between Capacitor Plates
slides.storyContext: One plate at +100 V, the other at 0 V, separated by 1 mm. What is the electric field?

example.solution: E = 100,000 V/m = 100 kV/m. This strong field is what pushes charges apart and stores energy.

slides.inSimpleWords: The voltage divided by the gap gives the field strength between parallel plates.

slides.title: What is a Capacitor?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator. When charged, one plate holds +Q, the other −Q. Potential difference U appears between them.

points.label: Capacitance C
points.text: Defined as C = Q / U, with units farads (F) = C/V. Higher C means the capacitor stores more charge for the same voltage.

points.label: Parallel plate capacitor
points.text: For two square plates of area A, separated by distance d with permittivity ε₀: C = ε₀ A / d. Larger area or smaller gap ⟹ larger capacitance.

example.problem: A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area A = 0.01 m^2 and separation d = 0.001 m. Find its capacitance. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10^-12 F/m)

slides.inSimpleWords: A capacitor is an electrical container. Its capacitance tells you how much charge it holds for each volt applied.

image.alt: What is a Capacitor? — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Charging a Capacitor
slides.storyContext: When Ravi connects a battery to a capacitor, charge flows from the battery onto the plates. Negative charge accumulates on one plate, positive on the other, until the voltage matches the battery. Then flow stops—the capacitor is 'charged.'

slides.title: Charge Stored in Flash Capacitor
slides.storyContext: A camera flash capacitor has C = 100 μF and is charged to 300 V.

example.solution: Q = 0.03 C = 30 millicoulombs. 30 mC is a lot of charge released in microseconds = very bright flash!

slides.inSimpleWords: Charge stored = capacitance × voltage. Higher voltage or capacitance = more charge stored.

slides.title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor

points.label: Energy formula
points.text: Energy U = (1/2) C V^2 = (1/2) Q V = (1/2) Q^2 / C. Measured in joules (J). The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates.

points.label: Energy density
points.text: Energy per unit volume in the field: u = (1/2) ε₀ E^2. For a parallel plate capacitor with field E = V/d, this gives U = (1/2) ε₀ E^2 × (A × d) = (1/2) ε₀ A V^2 / d.

points.label: Camera flash example
points.text: A tiny capacitor charged to 300 V with C = 100 μF stores U = (1/2) × 100 × 10^-6 × (300)^2 ≈ 4.5 J—enough to power a bright flash.

slides.inSimpleWords: The more you charge a capacitor (higher Q or V), the more energy it stores. That's why camera flashes are dangerous—they hold a punch!

image.alt: Energy Stored in a Capacitor — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Why Flash Is Dangerous
slides.storyContext: Ravi warns Anjali never to touch the terminals of a charged capacitor. '4.5 joules sounds small, but released through your body in microseconds is 4.5 megawatts of power—enough to cause a serious shock or burn.'

slides.title: Energy Comparison
slides.storyContext: How much energy is 4.5 J? Compare to everyday objects.

example.problem: 4.5 J released in 10 microseconds = power = energy / time = 4.5 / 10×10^-6.
example.solution: P = 4.5 × 10^5 = 450,000 watts = 450 kW. A typical microwave oven is 1 kW—this is 450 times more power!

slides.inSimpleWords: Capacitors release energy extremely fast. The power is much higher than steady energy flow.

slides.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel

points.label: Parallel connection
points.text: Capacitors share the same voltage U. Total capacitance: C_total = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + … (capacitances add). Larger total capacitance.

points.label: Series connection
points.text: Capacitors share the same charge Q. Voltage divides. Reciprocals add: 1/C_total = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + 1/C_3 + … Smaller total capacitance.

points.label: Analogy
points.text: Parallel is like adding tanks to a system—more storage. Series is like adding resistances—reduces flow.

example.problem: Two capacitors: C_1 = 2 μF and C_2 = 3 μF. Find total C in series and in parallel.
example.solution: Parallel: C_total = 2 + 3 = 5 μF. Series: 1/C_total = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, so C_total = 6/5 = 1.2 μF.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel capacitors act like bigger containers (C adds). Series capacitors act like a narrower pipe (1/C adds).

image.alt: Capacitors in Series and Parallel — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Building Bigger Capacitance
slides.storyContext: Ravi shows Anjali how engineers combine capacitors. To get high capacitance, they connect them in parallel (like joining tanks). To get high voltage rating, they use series.

slides.title: Dielectrics in Capacitors

points.label: Dielectric constant κ
points.text: When an insulator (dielectric) is placed between plates, the capacitance increases: C_dielectric = κ C_vacuum, where κ > 1 (e.g., κ = 2 for paper, κ = 80 for water).

points.label: Mechanism
points.text: The dielectric's molecules polarize in response to the field, creating an internal field that opposes the applied field, allowing more charge to accumulate.

points.label: Practical use
points.text: Dielectrics increase capacitance without changing plate area or separation. They also allow higher voltages before breakdown.

slides.inSimpleWords: Filling the gap with plastic, paper, or ceramic instead of air makes a capacitor store more charge—like packing more into the same container.

image.alt: Dielectrics in Capacitors — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Dielectric Effect
slides.storyContext: A capacitor with air gap has C = 100 pF. When mica (κ = 6) fills the gap, what is the new capacitance?

example.problem: C_new = κ × C_air = 6 × 100 = 600 pF.
example.solution: Mica increases capacitance by factor of 6. Same physical size, 6× more charge storage!

slides.inSimpleWords: Dielectric materials greatly increase capacitance. This is why real capacitors are filled with ceramics or films.

slides.title: Why Capacitors Are Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Anjali notices capacitors in her TV remote, phone charger, and even LED lights. Ravi explains: 'Capacitors smooth out power ripples, store energy for brief power surges, and filter signals. They're as essential as resistors in electronics.'

slides.title: Combining Capacitances
slides.storyContext: An engineer needs 10 μF but has three 5 μF capacitors. How should they connect them?

example.problem: Try parallel and series combinations.
example.solution: Parallel: all three → 5+5+5 = 15 μF (too much). Series: all three → 1/C = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 = 3/5, so C = 5/3 ≈ 1.67 μF (too little). Use two in parallel (= 10 μF) and don't use the third.

slides.inSimpleWords: Choose series/parallel based on whether you need more voltage rating or more capacitance.

slides.title: Solved Problem: Charging and Discharging

example.problem: A 10 μF capacitor is charged to 100 V, then connected across a 50 Ω resistor. How much energy is released? How long until it drops to 1 V?
example.solution: Initial energy U_i = (1/2) × 10 × 10^-6 × (100)^2 = 0.05 J. Energy released = 0.05 J. Discharge follows V(t) = V_0 e^(-t/RC), where RC = 50 × 10 × 10^-6 = 5 × 10^-4 s. Time to 1 V: 1 = 100 e^(-t/RC), so e^(-t/RC) = 0.01, giving t = RC × ln(100) ≈ 5 × 10^-4 × 4.6 ≈ 2.3 × 10^-3 s = 2.3 ms.

slides.inSimpleWords: When a capacitor discharges through a resistor, the voltage drops exponentially. A bigger capacitor or resistor means slower discharge.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Charging and Discharging — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Challenge: Flash Capacitor Power
slides.storyContext: A camera flash stores 5 J in a capacitor. It releases this energy in 0.5 milliseconds. What is the average power during the flash?

points.text: Power = Energy / Time.

example.solution: P = 5 / (5 × 10^-4) = 10,000 watts = 10 kW. The flash produces 10 kilowatts of power!

slides.inSimpleWords: Fast energy release creates huge power. That's why the flash is so bright.

points.text: A portable defibrillator must deliver 200 J of energy in one shock. The capacitor is charged to 4000 V. What capacitance C is needed? (Use U = (1/2) C V^2)

example.problem: Solve for C.

image.alt: Challenge: Designing a Defibrillator Capacitor — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

slides.title: Supercapacitors and Future Tech
slides.storyContext: Ravi shows Anjali a supercapacitor (1 farad!). 'These store enormous energy compared to regular capacitors. Electric vehicles use them to recover braking energy. In 20 years, they might replace some battery uses.'

slides.title: Supercapacitor Energy Storage
slides.storyContext: A supercapacitor with C = 1 F is charged to 3 V (safe voltage for electronics). How much energy does it store?

example.solution: U = (1/2) × 1 × (3)^2 = 4.5 J. Same energy as the camera flash, but stored safely!

slides.inSimpleWords: Supercapacitors pack more energy into the same formula by using huge capacitance.

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Electric potential V is work per unit charge; voltage is the potential difference U_AB = V_A − V_B.
Electric field E = −dV/dr is perpendicular to equipotential surfaces.
Capacitance C = Q / U measures charge storage; for parallel plates, C = ε₀ A / d.
Energy U = (1/2) C V^2 is stored in the electric field.
In parallel, C_total = C_1 + C_2; in series, 1/C_total = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2.
Dielectrics increase C by factor κ; they also allow higher voltages.

slides.inSimpleWords: Capacitors are electrical batteries that store energy in an electric field, release it instantly, and power flashy things like camera flashes and defibrillators.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

subject: Physics
title: Lights, Fans, and Ohm's Law
hook: Why does a 60 W bulb glow brighter than a 40 W bulb? Anjali rewires her desk lamp and discovers the science of electrical power.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student experimenting with home electrical circuits

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining Ohm's law and circuit analysis

slides.title: Current Electricity
slides.storyContext: Anjali plugs in two light bulbs and wonders: why is one brighter? Ravi says, 'It's all about current, resistance, and power.'

image.alt: Current Electricity — Current Electricity

slides.title: The Brightness Mystery
slides.storyContext: At her study desk in Bangalore, Anjali notices two identical 230 V lamps—one rated 60 W, the other 40 W. Both glow when plugged into the same outlet, but the 60 W lamp is visibly brighter. 'Why,' she asks Ravi, 'does one bulb burn brighter if they get the same voltage?' Ravi smiles. 'Because the bright one uses more current—and current, resistance, and power are the keys to understanding electricity.'

image.alt: The Brightness Mystery — Current Electricity

slides.title: Electric Current and Charge Flow

points.label: Current definition
points.text: Electric current I is the rate of charge flow: I = Q / t, measured in amperes (A) = coulombs per second (C/s). 1 A = 1 C/s.

points.label: Direction convention
points.text: Conventional current direction is the flow of positive charges (opposite to electron flow). Current flows from + to − through external circuits.

points.label: Current density
points.text: Current per unit area: J = I / A, measured in A/m^2. For a wire with cross-section A carrying current I, J = I/A.

image.alt: Electric Current and Charge Flow — Current Electricity

slides.inSimpleWords: Current is the flow of electrical charge. It's measured in amps—how many coulombs per second are moving through a wire.

slides.title: Ravi Demonstrates Current
slides.storyContext: Ravi sets up a simple circuit: a 10 V battery connected to a 100 Ω resistor. 'Watch the ammeter,' he says. The needle shows 0.1 A. 'That's current—charge flowing per second. If this wire has 1 mm² cross-section, the current density is 100,000 A/m². Thick wires distribute the load; thin ones get hot.'

slides.title: Current in a Home Circuit

example.problem: A 60 W incandescent bulb on a 230 V circuit (India standard). Find the current through it.
example.solution: From P = VI, we get I = P/V = 60/230 ≈ 0.26 A. This is the current flowing through the bulb's filament.

slides.inSimpleWords: A 60 W bulb draws about 0.26 amps from the wall. Higher wattage lamps draw more current.

slides.title: Ohm's Law and Resistance

points.label: Ohm's Law
points.text: Voltage V across a conductor is proportional to current I through it: V = I R, where R is resistance (ohms, Ω). Rearranged: I = V/R and R = V/I.

points.label: Resistance formula
points.text: For a wire: R = ρ L / A, where ρ is resistivity (Ω·m), L is length, and A is cross-sectional area. Longer wires have higher R; thicker wires have lower R.

points.label: Temperature dependence
points.text: Resistivity increases with temperature: ρ(T) = ρ_0 [1 + α(T − T_0)], where α is the temperature coefficient (∼ 0.004 K^-1 for copper).

example.problem: A copper wire has resistivity ρ = 1.7 × 10^-8 Ω·m, length L = 10 m, and cross-section A = 1 mm^2 = 10^-6 m^2. Find its resistance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Resistance is the wire's opposition to current flow. Longer or thinner wires resist more. Ohm's law ties voltage, current, and resistance together: V = IR.

image.alt: Ohm's Law and Resistance — Current Electricity

slides.title: Why Thick Wires Are Better
slides.storyContext: Anjali's home wiring uses 1.5 mm² copper. Ravi explains: 'Thinner wires resist more—current heats them. Your home's 15 A circuit breaker trips if current gets too high because thin wires would overheat and start a fire. That's why electricians use thick wires for high-current circuits.'

slides.title: Resistance of Home Wiring

example.problem: A copper wire 50 m long with cross-section 1 mm² runs from the circuit breaker to a room. Find its resistance.
example.solution: R = ρL/A = (1.7 × 10^-8 × 50) / (10^-6) = 8.5 × 10^-7 / 10^-6 = 0.85 Ω. Small but significant—voltage drop = IR = 0.26 × 0.85 ≈ 0.22 V for a 0.26 A bulb.

slides.inSimpleWords: Long wires add up to measurable resistance, dropping some voltage by the time it reaches the appliance.

slides.title: Resistors in Series and Parallel

points.label: Series
points.text: Resistors in series: same current through all, voltage divides. Total resistance R_total = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + … (resistances add).

points.label: Parallel
points.text: Resistors in parallel: same voltage across all, current divides. Reciprocals add: 1/R_total = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + 1/R_3 + …

points.label: Power in series vs parallel
points.text: In series, total power P = I^2 R_total splits among resistors: P_i = I^2 R_i. In parallel, resistors with lower R dissipate more power.

example.problem: Two resistors: R_1 = 10 Ω, R_2 = 20 Ω. Voltage across both = 30 V. Find total current and power if connected (a) in series, (b) in parallel.

slides.inSimpleWords: Series resistors block more (R adds). Parallel resistors reduce R (easier path). Parallel draws more current and dissipates more power.

image.alt: Resistors in Series and Parallel — Current Electricity

slides.title: Decorative Lights in Series
slides.storyContext: Anjali buys a string of decorative fairy lights. Ravi warns: 'Each bulb is tiny—in series, they share the voltage. One breaks, and the whole string goes dark because current can't flow. Modern strings use parallel bulbs instead, so one failure doesn't kill them all.'

slides.title: Series vs Parallel: Which is Better?

points.text: Design a circuit: you have four 40 Ω resistors and a 120 V battery. Should you connect them in series or parallel to maximize power dissipation? Calculate the power in each case.

example.problem: Find total power in series and parallel.
example.solution: Series: R_total = 160 Ω, I = 120/160 = 0.75 A, P = 120 × 0.75 = 90 W. Parallel: 1/R = 4 × (1/40) = 0.1, R = 10 Ω, I = 120/10 = 12 A, P = 120 × 12 = 1440 W. Parallel dissipates 16× more power!

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel circuits dissipate much more power because resistance is lower, so current flows more freely.

slides.title: Electrical Power and Energy

points.label: Power formula
points.text: Power P = V I (watts, W). Also P = I^2 R = V^2 / R. 1 watt = 1 joule/second.

points.label: Energy
points.text: Energy consumed over time t: E = P t (joules). Home meters measure kilowatt-hours (kWh): 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10^6 J.

points.label: Heat dissipation
points.text: In a resistor, electrical energy converts to heat: Q = I^2 R t. This is why wires heat up when current flows.

slides.inSimpleWords: Power is how fast energy is used. Higher voltage or current means more power. Energy = power × time, measured in kWh for your home bill.

image.alt: Electrical Power and Energy — Current Electricity

slides.title: Anjali's Monthly Electricity Bill
slides.storyContext: Anjali looks at her home's power meter and monthly bill. It says 150 kWh used, at Rs 8 per kWh = Rs 1200. Ravi explains: 'A kilowatt-hour is the energy a 1000 W appliance uses in 1 hour. Your fan (500 W × 4 hours/day) consumes 2 kWh daily. Multiply by 30 days = 60 kWh per month, just for the fan!'

slides.title: Energy Cost for a Microwave

example.problem: A 1000 W microwave runs 30 min/day for 30 days. Cost is Rs 6 per kWh. Find total energy and cost.
example.solution: Power = 1000 W = 1 kW. Daily energy = 1 × 0.5 = 0.5 kWh. Monthly energy = 0.5 × 30 = 15 kWh. Cost = 15 × 6 = Rs 90.

slides.inSimpleWords: Higher wattage appliances use more power and cost more to run. Always check a device's wattage to estimate its electricity bill impact.

slides.title: Electromotive Force and Internal Resistance

points.label: EMF (ε)
points.text: Electromotive force is the non-conservative force that drives current around a circuit. It's not actually a force—it's energy per unit charge, measured in volts.

points.label: Internal resistance r
points.text: Real batteries have internal resistance r. Terminal voltage V = ε − I r (ε is EMF, r is internal resistance).

points.label: Circuit equation
points.text: For a battery ε, internal resistance r, external resistance R: I = ε / (R + r), and terminal voltage V = ε − I r.

example.problem: A 12 V battery with internal resistance r = 0.5 Ω is connected to an external load R = 11.5 Ω. Find current and terminal voltage.

slides.inSimpleWords: A battery's EMF is the energy it gives per coulomb of charge. But inside, resistance drops some voltage, so the terminal voltage is less.

image.alt: Electromotive Force and Internal Resistance — Current Electricity

slides.title: Why Phone Chargers Get Hot
slides.storyContext: Anjali notices her phone charger gets warm. Ravi explains: 'The charger's internal resistance dissipates power as heat. A 5 V, 2 A charger has internal resistance ~0.1 Ω. Heat dissipated = I^2 r = 4 × 0.1 = 0.4 W. Small, but spread over the tiny charger, it feels warm.'

slides.title: Battery Terminal Voltage Under Load

example.problem: A car battery rated 12 V with r = 0.05 Ω powers a starter motor (R ≈ 0.5 Ω). Find the terminal voltage and power delivered to the motor.
example.solution: I = 12 / (0.5 + 0.05) = 12 / 0.55 ≈ 21.8 A. Terminal voltage V = 12 − 21.8 × 0.05 ≈ 10.9 V. Power to motor P = V × I = 10.9 × 21.8 ≈ 237 W. (Starter current is very high; notice the voltage sag.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Under heavy load, a battery's terminal voltage drops because of internal resistance. Old batteries with high r sag even more.

slides.title: Solved Problem: Bulb Brightness Revisited

example.problem: A 60 W bulb and a 40 W bulb are both rated 230 V. Find the resistance of each. When both are plugged into 230 V mains, which dissipates more current?
example.solution: P = V^2 / R, so R = V^2 / P. For 60 W: R_60 = (230)^2 / 60 = 52900 / 60 ≈ 881.67 Ω. For 40 W: R_40 = (230)^2 / 40 = 52900 / 40 = 1322.5 Ω. The 60 W bulb has lower resistance. Current through 60 W: I = 230 / 881.67 ≈ 0.26 A. Current through 40 W: I = 230 / 1322.5 ≈ 0.17 A. The 60 W bulb draws more current, so it's brighter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Higher wattage means lower resistance. Lower resistance means more current flows, making the bulb hotter and brighter.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Bulb Brightness Revisited — Current Electricity

points.text: Anjali's home uses: 5 bulbs × 60 W each = 300 W (8 hours/day), 1 refrigerator 500 W (24 hours/day), and 1 geyser 2000 W (1 hour/day). Monthly electricity cost is 8 rupees per kWh. What is the monthly bill? (Assume 30 days.)

example.problem: Calculate total energy and cost.
example.solution: Bulbs: 0.3 kW × 8 × 30 = 72 kWh. Refrigerator: 0.5 kW × 24 × 30 = 360 kWh. Geyser: 2 kW × 1 × 30 = 60 kWh. Total = 72 + 360 + 60 = 492 kWh. Cost = 492 × 8 = Rs 3,936.

image.alt: Challenge: Energy Bill Calculation — Current Electricity

slides.title: Challenge: Fuse Rating for a Circuit

points.text: A room in Anjali's house has 5 bulbs (60 W each), an AC (1500 W), and a fan (100 W), all on one 15 A circuit breaker. If all devices run simultaneously, does the current exceed the circuit limit?

example.problem: Calculate total power and current at 230 V.
example.solution: Total power = 5 × 60 + 1500 + 100 = 300 + 1500 + 100 = 1900 W. Current I = P/V = 1900/230 ≈ 8.26 A. This is under 15 A, so the breaker won't trip—the circuit is safe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Circuit breakers trip if current exceeds a limit (15 A, 20 A, 30 A), protecting wires from overheating. Calculate total power and divide by voltage to check current.

slides.title: Real-World Power Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anjali tries to run her geyser (2000 W), AC (1500 W), and water pump (500 W) simultaneously. The 15 A breaker trips. 'Why?' she asks. Ravi does the math: 'Total power = 4000 W. Current = 4000/230 ≈ 17.4 A. Your breaker is rated 15 A, so it trips to protect the wires from melting. You'd need a 20 A circuit for all three.'

slides.title: Temperature Rise in Overloaded Wire

example.problem: A 1 mm² copper wire carries 20 A (overloaded). Temperature coefficient α = 0.004 K^-1. How much does its resistance increase if temperature rises from 20 °C to 50 °C?
example.solution: At 20 °C: R_0 ≈ 0.017 Ω/meter. At 50 °C: R = R_0 [1 + α(50 − 20)] = R_0 [1 + 0.004 × 30] = R_0 × 1.12. Resistance increases 12%. Power dissipated = I^2 R increases, heating the wire further—risk of fire.

slides.inSimpleWords: Overloaded wires heat up, their resistance increases, dissipating even more heat—a dangerous positive feedback loop.

slides.title: Challenge: Efficiency of Power Transmission

points.text: A power plant sends 1 MW at 10 kV through a transmission line with total resistance 10 Ω. How much power is lost to heat? What if the voltage is stepped up to 100 kV?

example.problem: Calculate power loss at each voltage.
example.solution: At 10 kV: I = P/V = 10^6 / 10^4 = 100 A. Loss = I^2 R = 100^2 × 10 = 100,000 W = 100 kW (10% loss). At 100 kV: I = 10^6 / 10^5 = 10 A. Loss = 10^2 × 10 = 1000 W = 1 kW (0.1% loss). Higher voltage drastically reduces loss!

slides.inSimpleWords: Transmission lines use high voltage and low current to minimize losses. That's why power is stepped up with transformers, then stepped down for homes.

slides.title: How Transformers Work
slides.storyContext: Anjali learns how transformers change voltage. Ravi explains: 'A transformer has two coils wound around an iron core. AC current in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field. This field passes through the iron to the secondary coil, inducing voltage there. Voltage ratio = turn ratio: V_secondary/V_primary = N_secondary/N_primary.'

slides.title: Transformer Voltage and Current

example.problem: A transformer steps down 230 V, 10 A (primary) to 12 V (secondary). Find turns ratio and secondary current.
example.solution: Turns ratio N_s/N_p = V_s/V_p = 12/230 ≈ 0.052 (about 1:20). Power in = Power out (ideal): V_p I_p = V_s I_s, so I_s = (230 × 10)/12 ≈ 192 A. High current, low voltage—perfect for charging.

slides.inSimpleWords: Transformers trade voltage for current. Step-down gives lower voltage but higher current; step-up is the opposite.

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Current I = Q/t (amps) is the rate of charge flow. Ohm's law: V = IR.
Resistance R = ρL/A depends on material, length, and cross-section.
Series: R_total = ΣR (same current); Parallel: 1/R_total = Σ(1/R) (same voltage).
Power P = VI = I^2 R = V^2/R; Energy E = Pt (kWh for homes).
EMF ε drives current; terminal voltage V = ε − Ir accounts for internal resistance.
Higher wattage bulbs have lower resistance and draw more current—that's why they glow brighter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electricity flows as current through resistances, carrying power. Ohm's law and series/parallel rules let you analyze any circuit.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Current Electricity

subject: Physics
title: Compass Needles and Cosmic Rays
hook: What makes a compass needle point north? Anjali discovers how moving charges create magnetic fields—and how the Earth is a giant magnet.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student investigating magnetism with household materials

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining Lorentz force and magnetic field geometry

slides.title: Moving Charges and Magnetism
slides.storyContext: Anjali plays with a compass and a wire carrying current. Ravi shows her that moving charges create magnetic fields—just like the Earth does.

image.alt: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: The Compass Deflection
slides.storyContext: In her home lab in Kolkata, Anjali sets a compass needle on her desk, pointing north. She holds a wire carrying electric current over the needle. To her amazement, the needle deflects! 'Why does a wire move the compass?' she asks. Ravi explains: 'Every moving charge creates a magnetic field. The Earth is magnetic because of currents deep in its iron core. Your wire's current field deflects the compass needle.'

image.alt: The Compass Deflection — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge

points.label: Lorentz force
points.text: A charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B experiences force F = q v × B (vector cross product). Magnitude: F = q v B sin(θ), where θ is angle between v and B.

points.label: Direction
points.text: Use right-hand rule: fingers point along v, curl toward B, thumb points along F. For negative charge, reverse.

points.label: Unit
points.text: Magnetic field B is measured in tesla (T) = kg/(A·s^2). 1 tesla is strong (Earth's field ≈ 50 μT).

image.alt: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.inSimpleWords: A moving charge in a magnetic field feels a sideways push—perpendicular to both its motion and the field.

slides.title: Ravi Demonstrates with a Magnet and Wire
slides.storyContext: Ravi sets up a current-carrying wire through a strong neodymium magnet. 'Watch,' he says, switching on current. The wire jerks sideways! 'That's the Lorentz force. The heavier the charge or current, the faster it moves, and the stronger the field—the bigger the force.'

slides.title: Lorentz Force on an Electron

example.problem: An electron (q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C) moves at v = 10^5 m/s perpendicular to B = 0.5 T. Find the magnetic force.
example.solution: F = qvB = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 10^5 × 0.5 = 8 × 10^-15 N. Tiny force, but on a tiny particle—huge acceleration!

slides.inSimpleWords: Fast-moving charges in strong fields experience strong sideways forces. This is how particle accelerators and CRT screens work.

slides.title: Circular Motion in a Magnetic Field

points.label: Perpendicular motion
points.text: When v ⊥ B, the magnetic force provides centripetal acceleration. Charge moves in a circle with radius r = m v / (q B).

points.label: Cyclotron frequency
points.text: Angular frequency ω = q B / m (rad/s). Period T = 2π / ω = 2πm / (qB). Frequency f = 1/T = qB / (2πm).

points.label: Application: Mass spectrometry
points.text: Ions of different mass-to-charge ratios (m/q) follow different radii in the same B field. This separates isotopes and identifies molecules.

example.problem: An electron (m = 9.1 × 10^-31 kg, q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C) moves perpendicular to B = 0.1 T at v = 10^6 m/s. Find radius and period.

slides.inSimpleWords: A charged particle in a perpendicular magnetic field spirals in circles—the smaller the charge-to-mass ratio, the bigger the circle.

image.alt: Circular Motion in a Magnetic Field — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Inside the Cyclotron
slides.storyContext: Anjali learns about particle accelerators. Ravi explains: 'A cyclotron is a machine that spirals charged particles in circles with an increasing-strength magnetic field. Each loop they spiral tighter, moving faster. By the time they exit, they've gained enormous energy—used in hospitals for cancer therapy.'

slides.title: Magnetic Field from a Current-Carrying Wire

points.label: Biot-Savart Law (qualitative)
points.text: A current-carrying segment creates a magnetic field. Field circles around the wire (right-hand rule: thumb along current, fingers curl in B direction).

points.label: Long straight wire
points.text: Magnetic field at distance r from wire: B = μ₀ I / (2π r), where μ₀ = 4π × 10^-7 T·m/A (permeability of free space).

points.label: Circular loop
points.text: At the center of a loop of radius a carrying current I: B = μ₀ I / (2a). Field direction given by right-hand rule.

image.alt: Magnetic Field from a Current-Carrying Wire — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.inSimpleWords: Current creates circular magnetic fields. The closer to the wire, the stronger the field. Bigger current or tighter loop means stronger field.

slides.title: Magnetic Field Near a Power Line

example.problem: A power transmission line carries I = 1000 A. Find the magnetic field at 1 m distance.
example.solution: B = μ₀ I / (2π r) = (4π × 10^-7 × 1000) / (2π × 1) = (4 × 10^-4) / 2 = 2 × 10^-4 T = 200 μT. This is about 4× stronger than Earth's field!

slides.inSimpleWords: High-current transmission lines create strong magnetic fields around them. That's why utility companies recommend keeping houses away from power lines.

slides.title: Force Between Two Current-Carrying Wires

points.label: Ampère's force law
points.text: Two parallel wires carrying currents I₁ and I₂ separated by distance d experience force per unit length: F/L = μ₀ I₁ I₂ / (2π d).

points.label: Same direction = attraction
points.text: Currents in same direction attract; opposite currents repel.

points.label: Ampere (unit definition)
points.text: The ampere is defined so that two parallel wires 1 m apart, each carrying 1 A, experience a force of 2 × 10^-7 N per meter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wires with current push or pull each other magnetically. Same-direction currents attract like friends; opposite currents repel like enemies.

image.alt: Force Between Two Current-Carrying Wires — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Challenge: Magnetic Force Between Cables

points.text: Two parallel cables, 5 cm apart, carry 100 A each in the same direction. Find the force per meter between them. Is it attractive or repulsive?

example.problem: Calculate F/L using Ampère's law.
example.solution: F/L = μ₀ I₁ I₂ / (2π d) = (4π × 10^-7 × 100 × 100) / (2π × 0.05) = (4 × 10^-3) / 0.1 = 0.04 N/m = 4 N per 100 m. Attractive (currents same direction).

slides.inSimpleWords: High-current cables attract each other strongly. This can cause cables to twist or fail in power systems if not properly separated.

slides.title: Motors and Lorentz Force
slides.storyContext: Anjali examines an electric motor. Ravi points to the coil: 'Current flows through this wire in a magnetic field. Each side of the coil experiences F = IL × B in opposite directions—creating a torque. Spin the coil faster, and it turns the shaft. That's how motors work—pure Lorentz force.'

slides.title: Force on a Motor Wire

example.problem: A motor wire 10 cm long carries 5 A perpendicular to B = 0.2 T. Find force on the wire.
example.solution: F = I L B sin(90°) = 5 × 0.1 × 0.2 × 1 = 0.1 N. Small force, but with many coils and high field, motors produce significant torque.

slides.inSimpleWords: Current-carrying wires in magnetic fields experience forces. Arrange many wires in a coil, and you get rotating motion—electric motors.

slides.title: Solenoid and Magnetic Dipole

points.label: Solenoid
points.text: A coil of wire wound around a cylinder. Inside, magnetic field B ≈ μ₀ n I, where n = N/L is turns per unit length, I is current.

points.label: Magnetic dipole moment
points.text: For a current loop: μ = N I A, where N is number of turns, A is loop area. Dipole moment is a vector pointing out via right-hand rule.

points.label: Torque in external field
points.text: A magnetic dipole in field B experiences torque τ = μ × B. Magnitude τ = μ B sin(θ). Dipole aligns with field (lowest energy).

example.problem: A solenoid has N = 1000 turns, length L = 0.2 m, and carries I = 2 A. Find field inside.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wrap wire in a coil and current flows through it: you make a solenoid, a tiny electromagnet. More turns or more current = stronger field.

image.alt: Solenoid and Magnetic Dipole — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Electromagnets in Doorbells
slides.storyContext: Anjali presses her doorbell. Ravi explains: 'Inside is a solenoid—coil of wire around an iron core. When current flows, the magnetic field pulls an iron armature, ringing the bell. When current stops, a spring returns the armature. Simple, but brilliant.'

slides.title: Charging a Smartphone and Wireless Power
slides.storyContext: Anjali notices wireless charging pads. Ravi says: 'A coil in the charger creates an AC magnetic field. A second coil in your phone sits in this field. The changing field induces current in the phone coil—Faraday induction. The closer the phones, the stronger the coupling. That's wireless power transfer.'

slides.title: Magnetic Moment of a Current Loop

example.problem: A coil with 50 turns, area 0.01 m², carries 2 A current. Find its magnetic moment.
example.solution: μ = N I A = 50 × 2 × 0.01 = 1 A·m². This dipole will experience strong torque in an external field.

slides.inSimpleWords: The magnetic moment determines how strongly a current loop aligns with external fields. Larger loops, more turns, or higher current = larger moment.

slides.title: Solved Problem: Magnetic Deflection in a CRT

example.problem: In a cathode-ray tube (old TV), an electron (v = 10^7 m/s) enters a uniform magnetic field B = 0.01 T perpendicular to velocity. The deflection region is 0.05 m long. Find deflection angle.
example.solution: Radius of curvature r = mv/(qB) = (9.1 × 10^-31 × 10^7) / (1.6 × 10^-19 × 0.01) ≈ 0.057 m. Arc length in field s = 0.05 m. Deflection angle θ = s/r = 0.05/0.057 ≈ 0.88 rad ≈ 50 degrees.

slides.inSimpleWords: A beam of electrons or other charged particles bends in a magnetic field, like light bending in a lens. Stronger field or slower particles bend more sharply.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Magnetic Deflection in a CRT — Moving Charges and Magnetism

points.text: Earth's magnetic field strength at the equator is approximately 30 μT. A compass needle (magnetic dipole moment μ = 0.1 A·m^2) aligns with the field. What torque does the field exert on the needle if it's tilted 45° from north?

example.problem: Calculate the torque.

image.alt: Challenge: Earth's Magnetic Field — Moving Charges and Magnetism

slides.title: Challenge: Designing a Solenoid Magnet

points.text: You need to design a solenoid that produces B = 0.02 T inside. The wire can carry max 5 A, and the solenoid is 10 cm long. How many turns do you need? (Assume μ₀ ≈ 4π × 10^-7 T·m/A.)

example.problem: Find N given B, I, and L.
example.solution: B = μ₀ n I = μ₀ (N/L) I. So N = BL / (μ₀ I) = (0.02 × 0.1) / (4π × 10^-7 × 5) = 0.002 / (2π × 10^-6) ≈ 318 turns. Practical design.

slides.inSimpleWords: To make a stronger solenoid, use more turns, higher current, or shorter length. Trade-offs between difficulty and strength.

slides.title: Challenge: Relativity and Magnetism

points.text: A mysterious fact: magnetism is actually a relativistic effect! An electron moving parallel to a wire with current experiences a magnetic force. But in the electron's rest frame, the wire appears to move—creating an electric field that pushes the electron. Both descriptions agree: same force. Why?

example.problem: Explain the relativity of magnetism.
example.solution: In the lab frame: Lorentz force F = q v × B acts on the moving electron. In the electron's frame: the wire's positive ions and electrons both move, but due to length contraction, their densities differ—creating a net electric field E that pushes the electron. Transformations of E and B under relativity make both descriptions consistent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetism is electricity seen from a moving viewpoint. Relativity ensures electric and magnetic forces transform correctly between observers.

slides.title: Electromagnets in Scrapyards
slides.storyContext: Anjali watches a video of a massive electromagnet lifting cars at a scrapyard. Ravi explains: 'That's a solenoid around an iron core. When current flows, the core amplifies the field 1000×. Shut off current, and the magnet releases—genius design for moving metal.'

slides.title: Challenge: Magnetic Field Inside vs Outside

points.text: A long solenoid (N = 5000 turns, L = 0.5 m, I = 1 A) has an iron core (μ_r = 1000). Calculate B inside and just outside the core.

example.problem: Find B inside and outside.
example.solution: Inside: B = μ₀ μ_r n I = (4π × 10^-7) × 1000 × (5000/0.5) × 1 ≈ 12.6 T. Outside (far from ends): B ≈ 0 (field lines close through the iron, don't leak out). The iron confines the field.

slides.inSimpleWords: Iron cores concentrate magnetic fields inside the solenoid. Field lines don't leak out much, making electromagnets efficient and focused.

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Lorentz force F = qv × B acts perpendicular to both velocity and magnetic field.
Charged particles in perpendicular B fields move in circles with radius r = mv/(qB).
Current-carrying wires create circular magnetic fields: B = μ₀I/(2πr) for straight wire, B = μ₀I/(2a) at center of loop.
Parallel wires with same-direction currents attract; opposite currents repel.
A solenoid's field B = μ₀nI depends on turn density and current.
Magnetic dipoles (like compass needles) experience torque in external fields and align to lowest energy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Moving charges create magnetic fields, and magnetic fields push moving charges sideways. This powers motors, compasses, and all electromagnetic devices.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Moving Charges and Magnetism

subject: Physics
title: Iron Filings and Permanent Magnets
hook: Why is iron magnetic when iron atoms are neutral? Anjali learns how atomic currents and spin create permanent magnets.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student experimenting with magnets and magnetic materials

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining atomic magnetism and magnetic domains

slides.title: Magnetism and Matter
slides.storyContext: Iron filings arrange in lines around a magnet. Ravi tells Anjali: 'Inside every iron atom, electrons spin like tiny planets, creating invisible magnetic fields.'

image.alt: Magnetism and Matter — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: The Iron Filing Pattern
slides.storyContext: Anjali sprinkles iron filings on paper above a bar magnet. They arrange in beautiful curved lines. 'The fields are invisible,' Ravi explains, 'but iron is ferromagnetic—its atoms have unpaired electrons that spin, creating tiny magnetic dipoles. When billions align, they make a strong magnet.'

image.alt: The Iron Filing Pattern — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Atomic Magnetism

points.label: Bohr magneton
points.text: The fundamental unit of atomic magnetic moment: μ_B = e ℏ / (2 m_e) ≈ 9.27 × 10^-24 J/T, where e is electron charge, ℏ is reduced Planck's constant.

points.label: Orbital and spin magnetism
points.text: Electrons create magnetic moments two ways: (1) orbital angular momentum L, giving μ_L = −(e/2m_e) L; (2) intrinsic spin S, giving μ_S = −(e/m_e) S ≈ −2 μ_B (g-factor ≈ 2).

points.label: Net moment per atom
points.text: Total atomic dipole moment μ = μ_L + μ_S. For closed shells (like noble gases), L = S = 0, so μ = 0. Unpaired electrons give non-zero μ.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electrons spin like tops and orbit like planets, each motion creating a tiny magnet. Many electrons spinning together add up to strong magnetism.

image.alt: Atomic Magnetism — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Why Some Elements Are Magnetic
slides.storyContext: Anjali learns the electron configuration of iron: [Ar] 3d^6 4s^2. 'Those six 3d electrons have four unpaired spins,' Ravi explains. 'Each unpaired electron carries a Bohr magneton of magnetic moment. Add billions of iron atoms with their spins aligned, and you get a permanent magnet strong enough to hold a door open.'

slides.title: Magnetic Moment of an Iron Atom

example.problem: An iron atom has 4 unpaired d-electrons, each contributing ~1 Bohr magneton. Estimate its total magnetic moment in J/T.
example.solution: μ ≈ 4 × μ_B = 4 × 9.27 × 10^-24 ≈ 3.7 × 10^-23 J/T. A tiny magnet, but multiply by ~10^23 atoms/cm³, and you get macroscopic magnetism.

slides.inSimpleWords: Each iron atom acts like a tiny magnet. When trillions align, their moments add up to strong magnetism.

slides.title: Magnetization and Magnetic Field

points.label: Magnetization M
points.text: Magnetization is magnetic dipole moment per unit volume: M = Σμ / V, with units A/m. Total magnetic dipole moment of a sample: μ_sample = M × V.

points.label: Magnetic field B and auxiliary field H
points.text: In matter: B = μ₀ (H + M) = μ₀ μ_r H, where μ_r is relative permeability. In free space: B = μ₀ H.

points.label: Susceptibility χ
points.text: Magnetization is proportional to applied field: M = χ H, where χ is magnetic susceptibility (dimensionless). So B = μ₀ (1 + χ) H = μ₀ μ_r H.

image.alt: Magnetization and Magnetic Field — Magnetism and Matter

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetization M is how magnetized a material is per unit volume. The internal field B depends on both the applied field and the magnetization.

slides.title: Iron vs. Non-Magnetic Metals
slides.storyContext: Anjali tests whether aluminum and copper are attracted to magnets. They're not. Ravi says: 'Copper and aluminum have paired electrons—their magnetic moments cancel. Iron, cobalt, and nickel have unpaired d-electrons. That's the difference. Elements on the right side of the periodic table are usually ferromagnetic.'

slides.title: Ferromagnetism and Magnetic Domains

points.label: Ferromagnetism
points.text: In iron, cobalt, nickel: unpaired d-electrons create strong atomic moments. Exchange interaction causes parallel alignment even without external field.

points.label: Magnetic domains
points.text: Ferromagnetic materials consist of regions (domains) where atomic moments are aligned. Each domain acts like a tiny magnet. Unmagnetized material has random domain orientations; net M = 0.

points.label: Hysteresis
points.text: When external field is applied, domains align gradually. When field is removed, domains don't fully return—creating permanent magnetization (remanence). Heating above Curie temperature (1043 K for iron) destroys ferromagnetism.

image.alt: Ferromagnetism and Magnetic Domains — Magnetism and Matter

slides.inSimpleWords: Ferromagnetic materials have regions (domains) where atomic spins align. Applying a field rotates domains toward the field; some stay aligned, creating permanent magnets.

slides.title: Why Hitting a Magnet Weakens It
slides.storyContext: Anjali's older magnet is getting weaker. Ravi explains: 'Domains are fragile. Vibrations and shocks randomize them—like shuffling a deck of cards. Eventually, half point up and half point down, canceling each other. That's why magnets weaken over time. Heating above the Curie temperature destroys them completely.'

slides.title: Magnetization Under Applied Field

example.problem: A piece of unmagnetized iron (V = 1 cm³) is placed in a field H = 1000 A/m. If χ_iron ≈ 1000, find magnetization M and total field B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Iron amplifies an applied field by ~1000×. A weak field magnetizes iron strongly; domains rotate and add their moments.

slides.title: Paramagnetism and Diamagnetism

points.label: Paramagnetism
points.text: Materials with unpaired electrons (O₂, many transition metals, rare earths). Atomic moments have no preferred direction, but external field weakly aligns them. Susceptibility χ ≈ 10^-3 to 10^-5, temperature-dependent (Curie law: χ ∝ 1/T).

points.label: Diamagnetism
points.text: All materials have some diamagnetism (even copper, water). External field induces opposite-direction moments in electron orbits (Lenz's law). Susceptibility χ ≈ −10^-5 to −10^-6, temperature-independent. Opposed by stronger paramagnetism or ferromagnetism if present.

points.label: Superconductors
points.text: Perfect diamagnets below critical temperature: χ = −1, completely expel external B field (Meissner effect). Levitating magnets over superconductors are a classic demo.

slides.inSimpleWords: Paramagnetic materials are weakly attracted to magnetic fields. Diamagnetic materials are very weakly repelled. Superconductors are perfect diamagnets.

image.alt: Paramagnetism and Diamagnetism — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Diamagnetism and the Meissner Effect
slides.storyContext: Anjali watches a video of a magnet levitating above a superconductor. 'That's perfect diamagnetism,' Ravi says. 'Below the critical temperature, superconductors expel ALL magnetic field. Not just resisting field changes (that's resistance)—actually pushing field lines away. A magnet floats because it can't touch the superconductor's perfect field.'

slides.title: Paramagnetic Susceptibility

example.problem: Oxygen gas (O₂) is paramagnetic with χ = 2.1 × 10^-6. In a field H = 10^5 A/m, find magnetization.
example.solution: M = χ H = 2.1 × 10^-6 × 10^5 = 0.21 A/m. Tiny magnetization, but real—which is why O₂ is attracted to magnetic fields (and why MRI machines detect blood oxygenation).

slides.inSimpleWords: Paramagnetic materials like oxygen respond weakly to magnetic fields. Strong superconducting magnets in MRI machines use this principle.

slides.title: MRI Machines and Superconductors
slides.storyContext: Anjali learns how MRI works. Ravi explains: 'An MRI machine uses a superconducting electromagnet creating a 1-3 tesla field (20,000× Earth's field). Paramagnetic hydrogen nuclei in water align, then radio waves flip them. They relax back, emitting signals that build an image of your organs.'

slides.title: Hysteresis and Energy Loss

points.label: Hysteresis loop
points.text: Plot B vs H: increasing H increases B (curve bends up); at peak H, B saturates. Decreasing H, B doesn't retrace the same path—lag is hysteresis. At H = 0, remanent field B_r remains (permanent magnet).

points.label: Energy loss
points.text: Area enclosed by hysteresis loop = energy dissipated per cycle per unit volume. For AC-driven ferromagnetic cores (transformers, motors), this is core loss, converted to heat.

points.label: Soft vs hard magnetic materials
points.text: Soft iron: narrow hysteresis loop, easy to magnetize/demagnetize (transformer cores). Hard steel: wide loop, high remanence, hard to change (permanent magnets).

image.alt: Hysteresis and Energy Loss — Magnetism and Matter

slides.inSimpleWords: Hysteresis is the lag when magnetic field is switched. Energy is wasted flipping domains—reason transformers and motors get hot.

slides.title: Transformer Cores and Soft Iron
slides.storyContext: Anjali sees a power transformer with a laminated iron core. Ravi explains: 'We use soft iron because it has a thin hysteresis loop—easy to magnetize and demagnetize. At 50 Hz (India), the field reverses 50 times per second. Thick-walled loops would waste energy as heat. Also, we laminate (thin sheets) to reduce eddy currents—swirling currents that also waste power.'

slides.title: Hysteresis Loop Energy

example.problem: A transformer core loop encloses area 10^-2 A·m on the H-B graph. Volume is 0.1 m³. Energy dissipated per cycle = area × volume. If frequency is 50 Hz, find power loss.
example.solution: Energy/cycle = 10^-2 × 0.1 = 10^-3 J/cycle. Power = energy/cycle × frequency = 10^-3 × 50 = 0.05 W. Small, but adds up in large transformers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hysteresis waste energy as heat in transformers and motors. That's why they need cooling and why efficiency matters.

slides.title: Earth's Magnetism and Geomagnetism

points.label: Magnetic poles
points.text: Earth's magnetic dipole moment is ~7.9 × 10^15 A·m^2. Magnetic north pole is currently near geographic north pole (but off by ~11°, drifting slowly). South magnetic pole is in Antarctica.

points.label: Magnetic declination and inclination
points.text: Declination = angle between true north and magnetic north (varies by location, ~5° in India currently). Inclination (dip) = angle of B field below horizontal (∼45° in India).

points.label: Origin: liquid iron core
points.text: Slow convection of molten iron in Earth's outer core creates circulating currents, generating a dipole field via dynamo effect. Field reverses every ~200,000 years.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's iron core circulates like a coil of current, making our planet a giant magnet. Compass needles align with this field, pointing roughly north.

image.alt: Earth's Magnetism and Geomagnetism — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Magnetic Pole Reversals
slides.storyContext: Anjali learns that Earth's poles flip periodically. Ravi explains: 'Every ~200,000 years, magnetic north becomes south and vice versa. We see this in ocean floor rocks—magnetic reversals recorded in lava layers. The last one was ~800,000 years ago. Before you worry: the reversals take ~1000 years, and the field doesn't vanish—just gets weaker temporarily. Life survives them.'

slides.title: Solved Problem: Magnetization of Iron

example.problem: A sample of iron (volume V = 10 cm^3 = 10^-5 m^3) has relative permeability μ_r = 1000 in an applied field H = 1000 A/m. Find magnetization M and total field B.
example.solution: Susceptibility χ = μ_r − 1 = 999. Magnetization M = χ H = 999 × 1000 = 9.99 × 10^5 A/m. Field B = μ₀ μ_r H = (4π × 10^-7) × 1000 × 1000 = 4π × 10^-1 ≈ 1.26 T.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply a field to iron: magnetization is huge (factor of 1000) compared to vacuum. That's why iron cores strengthen electromagnets.

image.alt: Solved Problem: Magnetization of Iron — Magnetism and Matter

points.text: Iron loses ferromagnetism above its Curie temperature (1043 K). Why? A hint: thermal vibrations randomize atomic dipole orientations, competing with exchange interaction. Above T_C, entropy wins and ferromagnetism vanishes. Show that χ ≈ C/T (Curie law) for paramagnetism, where C is a material constant.

example.problem: Write Curie law and explain why heating destroys ferromagnetism.
example.solution: χ = C/T means susceptibility drops as T increases. Thermal energy ~kT random-orients spins faster than exchange interaction can align them. When kT_C ≈ exchange energy, order collapses and the material becomes paramagnetic. Below T_C, exchange is strong; above T_C, entropy dominates.

image.alt: Challenge: Curie Temperature — Magnetism and Matter

slides.title: Challenge: Magnetic Declination Navigation

points.text: In Delhi, magnetic declination is about 6° West (compass points 6° left of true north). If you hike using a compass that points magnetic north, how far east or west will you be after walking 10 km north?

example.problem: Calculate eastward error from declination.
example.solution: Angle error = 6° = 6π/180 = 0.105 rad. Eastward displacement ≈ 10 × sin(6°) ≈ 10 × 0.105 ≈ 1.05 km. You'll end up ~1 km west of your target.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic compasses don't point to true geographic north everywhere. Knowing local declination is crucial for accurate navigation.

slides.title: Migratory Birds and Earth's Magnetism
slides.storyContext: Anjali learns that birds navigate using Earth's magnetic field. Ravi explains: 'Many birds have magnetoreceptor proteins that align with B field lines. They sense inclination—the angle of field lines below horizontal. In India, it's ~45°. Birds use this like an internal compass to find south in winter.'

slides.title: Challenge: Magnetosphere and Solar Radiation

points.text: Earth's magnetosphere protects us from solar wind. Estimate the scale: Earth's field is ~30 μT at equator. Solar wind dynamic pressure is ~1 nPa. At what distance is magnetic pressure equal to dynamic pressure (magnetopause)?

example.problem: Find magnetopause distance.
example.solution: Magnetic energy density u_B = B^2 / (2μ₀). At magnetopause, u_B ≈ dynamic pressure P. For Earth's dipole, B ∝ 1/r^3 at equator. Solving yields r ≈ 10 Earth radii ≈ 64,000 km. This is where Earth's field pushes back solar wind.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's magnetic field extends into space, forming a protective bubble (magnetosphere). Without it, solar wind would strip our atmosphere.

slides.title: Northern Lights and Magnetic Storms
slides.storyContext: Anjali watches videos of the aurora borealis. Ravi explains: 'During solar storms, intense solar wind pushes the magnetosphere closer. Charged particles leak in along field lines near the poles, colliding with oxygen (green) and nitrogen (red). That's the aurora—Earth's magnetic field's light show.'

slides.title: What You've Learned

points.text: Atomic magnetism arises from electron orbital motion and spin; basic unit is Bohr magneton μ_B ≈ 9.27 × 10^-24 J/T.
Ferromagnetism (iron, cobalt, nickel): strong unpaired-electron moments with exchange interaction aligning them.
Magnetic domains: regions of aligned dipoles. Unmagnetized material has random domains; applied field rotates them, leaving remanence (permanent magnetism).
Hysteresis: lag between B and H, energy loss proportional to loop area.
Paramagnetism: weak alignment of existing dipoles (χ > 0). Diamagnetism: induced opposite moments (χ < 0).
Earth's magnetic field from circulating currents in liquid iron core; field reverses every ~200,000 years.

slides.inSimpleWords: Materials become magnets when atomic spins align. Ferromagnets have permanent alignment; others weakly align or repel. Heating destroys alignment by shaking atoms randomly.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Magnetism and Matter

subject: Physics
title: Faraday's Discovery: Making Power from Magnetism
hook: A changing magnetic field can generate electricity without a battery. Anjali swings a magnet near a coil and watches a meter jump.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student discovering electromagnetic induction with a coil and magnet

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining Faraday's law and Lenz's law

slides.title: Electromagnetic Induction
slides.storyContext: Anjali swings a bar magnet toward a coil connected to an ammeter. Mysteriously, the meter needle deflects—without any battery!

image.alt: Electromagnetic Induction — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.title: The Swinging Magnet
slides.storyContext: In her physics lab in Mumbai, Anjali holds a bar magnet near a coil wired to an ammeter. When she swings the magnet toward the coil, the meter jumps—current flows! When she holds the magnet still, the current stops. 'Ravi uncle, how can a magnet make electricity?' she asks. Ravi smiles: 'Faraday discovered that a *changing* magnetic field induces an electric field. This is the secret behind generators, transformers, and all AC power.'

image.alt: The Swinging Magnet — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.title: Magnetic Flux

points.label: Flux definition
points.text: Magnetic flux Φ (or Φ_B) is the magnetic field passing through a surface: Φ = ∫ B · dA. For uniform field perpendicular to area A: Φ = B A. Unit: weber (Wb) = tesla·m^2 (T·m^2).

points.label: Flux through a coil
points.text: For a coil with N turns, area A, in uniform field B at angle θ to normal: Φ = N B A cos(θ). Maximum when B is perpendicular to coil (θ = 0); zero when B is parallel to coil plane (θ = 90°).

points.label: Changing flux
points.text: Time-varying flux Φ(t) is key to induction. The rate of change dΦ/dt drives induced EMF.

image.alt: Magnetic Flux — Electromagnetic Induction

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic flux is how much field is threading through a surface. More field or bigger area means more flux. Angling the field reduces flux (cos effect).

slides.title: Worked Example: Flux Through a Rotating Coil

example.problem: A square coil with side 0.1 m (area A = 0.01 m²) rotates in a uniform magnetic field B = 2 T. The axis of rotation is perpendicular to B. At time t, the angle between B and the normal to the coil is θ(t) = ωt, where ω = 10 rad/s. Find the flux as a function of time and sketch it.
example.solution: Φ(t) = B A cos(θ(t)) = 2 × 0.01 × cos(10t) = 0.02 cos(10t) Wb. At t=0, Φ = 0.02 Wb (maximum). At t=π/20 s, θ = π/2, so Φ = 0 (field parallel to coil plane). At t=π/10 s, θ = π, so Φ = −0.02 Wb (reversed). The flux oscillates sinusoidally from +0.02 to −0.02 Wb with period T = 2π/ω ≈ 0.628 s.

slides.inSimpleWords: As a coil rotates, the flux through it oscillates. Maximum flux occurs when the field is perpendicular to the coil face; zero when parallel to the plane.

slides.title: Why Changing Flux Matters
slides.storyContext: Anjali tries an experiment: holding the magnet perfectly still near the coil. The ammeter shows zero. 'No current!' she exclaims. Ravi nods. 'Exactly, Anjali. A *static* magnetic field, no matter how strong, induces no current. But the moment you move the magnet—changing the flux—current flows. This is the heart of Faraday's law. Generators work by rotating a coil, changing the flux continuously, which drives a current. Static field = no induction. Changing field = induction. Simple rule.'

slides.title: Faraday's Law of Induction

points.label: The law
points.text: Induced EMF in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = −dΦ/dt. For N-turn coil: ε = −N dΦ/dt. Unit: volt (V).

points.label: Negative sign (Lenz's law insight)
points.text: The negative sign means induced EMF opposes the change in flux. If flux increases, induced EMF creates current to oppose it (pushes field out). If flux decreases, induced current tries to preserve it (pulls field in).

points.label: Physical interpretation
points.text: The induced EMF arises from a changing electric field generated by the changing magnetic field. This electric field accelerates charges in the circuit, creating current.

example.problem: A coil has N = 100 turns, area A = 0.02 m², and is in a uniform field B = 0.5 T perpendicular to the coil. The field decreases uniformly from 0.5 T to 0 T in Δt = 0.1 s. Find the induced EMF and direction (by Lenz's law).
example.solution: Initial flux Φ_i = N B A = 100 × 0.5 × 0.02 = 1 Wb. Final flux Φ_f = 0. Change ΔΦ = Φ_f − Φ_i = −1 Wb. Rate dΦ/dt = ΔΦ/Δt = −1/0.1 = −10 Wb/s. Induced EMF ε = −dΦ/dt = −(−10) = +10 V. Positive EMF means the induced current flows in a direction to create a magnetic field in the same direction as the decreasing external field (Lenz opposes the decrease).

slides.inSimpleWords: Faraday's law: changing magnetic flux generates electric voltage. Faster change means higher voltage. Lenz's law says the induced current always opposes the change.

slides.title: Lenz's Law in Action: The Magnetic Brake
slides.storyContext: Ravi pushes a magnet into a copper tube, and Anjali feels resistance—the magnet slows down dramatically! 'That's Lenz's law at work,' Ravi explains. 'The changing flux induces currents in the tube (eddy currents) that create a magnetic field opposing the magnet's motion. The magnet must do work against this opposition. Energy is neither lost nor gained; the kinetic energy of the magnet converts to heat in the tube's resistance. This is how magnetic brakes work in trains and elevators!'

slides.title: Worked Example: EMF in a Moving Conductor

example.problem: A conducting rod of length L = 0.5 m slides along parallel rails separated by 0.5 m in a perpendicular magnetic field B = 1 T. The rod moves with constant velocity v = 2 m/s. Calculate the motional EMF, current (circuit resistance R = 10 Ω), and the magnetic force on the rod.
example.solution: Motional EMF: ε = B L v = 1 × 0.5 × 2 = 1 V. Current: I = ε/R = 1/10 = 0.1 A. Force on rod: F = B I L = 1 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.05 N (opposing motion). Power: P_mech = F × v = 0.05 × 2 = 0.1 W (work input). P_elec = I² R = (0.1)² × 10 = 0.1 W (dissipated). Energy is conserved: mechanical work input = electrical energy dissipated.

slides.inSimpleWords: Moving a conductor perpendicular to a magnetic field induces voltage (EMF = BLv). The resulting current experiences a force opposing the motion, so you must do work to keep it moving.

slides.title: Motional EMF and AC Generators

points.label: Simple motional EMF
points.text: A rod of length L moving perpendicular to B with velocity v generates EMF = B L v.

points.label: Rotating coil (AC generator)
points.text: A rectangular coil (N turns, area A) rotates in uniform B field. Flux Φ(t) = NBA cos(ωt) where ω = 2πf. Induced EMF ε(t) = NBA ω sin(ωt) = ε₀ sin(ωt) with peak ε₀ = NBA ω.

points.label: Generator equations
points.text: ε₀ = NBA × 2πf. For India (f = 50 Hz): ε₀ = NBA × 314. RMS voltage ε_rms = ε₀ / √2. Home voltage 230 V RMS → peak ≈ 325 V.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spinning a coil in a magnetic field generates alternating voltage. Faster spin or stronger field means higher peak voltage. This is how power plants make electricity.

slides.title: Worked Example: AC Generator Output

example.problem: A generator has N = 500 turns, A = 0.1 m², B = 0.8 T, rotating at f = 50 Hz. Calculate peak EMF, RMS EMF, and the current delivered to a 100 Ω load.
example.solution: Peak EMF: ε₀ = NBA × 2πf = 500 × 0.8 × 0.1 × 2π × 50 ≈ 500 × 0.8 × 0.1 × 314 = 12,560 V ≈ 12.6 kV. RMS EMF: ε_rms = ε₀/√2 ≈ 8.9 kV. Current (at RMS): I_rms = ε_rms / R = 8900 / 100 = 89 A. This voltage would power many homes after stepping down through transformers.

slides.inSimpleWords: AC generators produce voltage proportional to the number of turns, magnetic field strength, coil area, and rotation speed. Faster rotation or more turns means higher voltage.

slides.title: Self-Inductance and Back-EMF

points.label: Self-inductance L
points.text: When current I in a coil changes, it creates changing flux through itself, inducing a back-EMF: ε_back = −L (dI/dt). L = N Φ / I (henries, H). Opposes the change (Lenz's law).

points.label: Practical consequence
points.text: Inductors resist sudden changes in current. Switching off an inductive circuit abruptly can generate dangerous voltage spikes.

points.label: Energy storage
points.text: Inductor stores magnetic energy: U = (1/2) L I². This energy must be dissipated or converted when the circuit is broken.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inductors store energy in their magnetic field and resist changes in current. Suddenly breaking an inductive circuit releases stored energy as a high voltage spike.

slides.title: Worked Example: Inductor Voltage Spike

example.problem: An inductor with L = 0.2 H carries steady current I = 5 A. If the current is suddenly cut off in Δt = 0.01 s, calculate the induced back-EMF and the energy released.
example.solution: Back-EMF magnitude: |ε_back| = L |dI/dt| = 0.2 × (5/0.01) = 0.2 × 500 = 100 V. Energy stored: U = (1/2) L I² = 0.5 × 0.2 × (5)² = 2.5 J. This high voltage (100 V) appears across the switching device when the circuit breaks, potentially causing arcing or damping. The 2.5 J must dissipate as heat, spark, or electromagnetic radiation—dangerous if not managed!

slides.inSimpleWords: Cutting current through an inductor creates a high voltage spike. Industrial switches use protection circuits (diodes, resistors) to safely dissipate this energy.

slides.title: Mutual Inductance and Transformers

points.label: Mutual inductance M
points.text: Primary coil (N_p turns) carries current I_p, creating flux Φ through secondary coil (N_s turns). Secondary EMF: ε_s = −M (dI_p/dt). M = N_s Φ / I_p (henries).

points.label: Transformer principle
points.text: Ideal transformer couples primary and secondary through shared flux. Voltage ratio: V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p. Current ratio: I_s / I_p = N_p / N_s (inverse).

points.label: Power conservation
points.text: Ideal transformer conserves power: V_p I_p = V_s I_s. No power loss in coupling or core (unrealistic but useful approximation).

slides.inSimpleWords: Transformers scale voltage and current for efficient transmission and safe distribution. Step-up transformers increase voltage (decrease current) for long-distance transmission; step-down transformers reduce voltage for homes.

slides.title: Worked Example: Transformer Design

example.problem: A transformer steps down 230 V AC to 12 V AC. Primary has N_p = 1000 turns. (a) Find secondary turns N_s. (b) If primary draws I_p = 1 A, find secondary current and power. (c) Compare to non-ideal transformer with 5% loss.
example.solution: (a) N_s = N_p × (V_s/V_p) = 1000 × (12/230) ≈ 52 turns. (b) Ideal: I_s = V_p I_p / V_s = 230 × 1 / 12 ≈ 19.2 A. Power: P = V_s I_s = 12 × 19.2 = 230 W. (c) Non-ideal with 5% loss: P_out = 230 × (1 − 0.05) = 218.5 W. I_s = 218.5 / 12 ≈ 18.2 A. Real transformers lose power to core heating and wire resistance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Transformers scale voltage inversely with current. A step-down 230V→12V transformer increases current by the inverse ratio (~19×). Real transformers have 90-99% efficiency.

slides.title: Worked Example: Induced EMF in a Sliding Loop

example.problem: A rectangular loop (length L = 0.3 m, width w = 0.2 m) moves at velocity v = 2 m/s into a perpendicular magnetic field B = 1.5 T. Calculate the induced EMF as the loop enters the field (leading edge cutting field lines) and when fully inside (no change).
example.solution: Leading edge entering: EMF = B L v = 1.5 × 0.3 × 2 = 0.9 V (voltage induced as the front of loop cuts field). Fully inside: dΦ/dt = 0 (flux constant once fully in), so EMF = 0 V. This explains why motors generate back-EMF only during acceleration or deceleration, not at constant speed.

slides.inSimpleWords: EMF is induced whenever flux changes. As a conductor cuts field lines (entering or leaving), EMF is generated. Once fully in a uniform field moving steadily, no more EMF.

slides.title: Wireless Power Transfer
slides.storyContext: Anjali's new phone has wireless charging—no cable! Ravi explains: 'A coil in the charger creates a time-varying magnetic field. Your phone's receiver coil detects the changing flux and, by Faraday's law, generates current to charge the battery. Same principle as a transformer, but with air gap instead of iron core. Induction across space.'

slides.title: Wireless Power Transfer via Mutual Inductance

points.label: Mutual inductance M
points.text: Primary coil (transmitter) oscillates at frequency f. Secondary coil (receiver) in its magnetic field experiences changing flux, inducing EMF ε = −M dI/dt.

points.label: Coupling coefficient
points.text: k = M / √(L₁L₂). For air gap: k ~ 0.1–0.3 (loose coupling). For iron core: k ~ 0.95 (tight coupling, like transformer).

points.label: Efficiency
